claim: Neurons in sensory cortex are tuned to diverse features in natural scenes.
source: Neurons in sensory cortex are tuned to diverse features in natural scenes.
evidence: This is a general statement about sensory cortex neurons that is supported by established scientific knowledge in neuroscience.

claim: The temporal prediction model was tested using simple feedforward neural networks trained to predict the next few moments of video or audio in clips of natural scenes.
source: We tested this hypothesis using simple feedforward neural networks, which were trained to predict the next few moments of video or audio in clips of natural scenes.
evidence: The manuscript describes the experimental methodology used to test the hypothesis.

claim: The networks developed receptive fields that closely matched those of real cortical neurons in different mammalian species.
source: The networks developed receptive fields that closely matched those of real cortical neurons in different mammalian species, including the oriented spatial tuning of primary visual cortex, the frequency selectivity of primary auditory cortex and, most notably, their temporal tuning properties.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on comparisons between model and experimental data.

claim: The better a network predicted future inputs, the more closely its receptive fields resembled those in the brain.
source: Furthermore, the better a network predicted future inputs the more closely its receptive fields resembled those in the brain.
evidence: This is a key finding based on quantitative analysis of the relationship between prediction error and similarity to neural data.

claim: Sensory processing is optimized to extract features with the most capacity to predict future input.
source: This suggests that sensory processing is optimized to extract those features with the most capacity to predict future input.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the finding that better prediction correlates with greater similarity to neural receptive fields.

claim: To strike a cricket ball, one must estimate its future location, not where it is now.
source: To strike a cricket ball, for example, one must estimate its future location, not where it is now (Nijhawan, 1994).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Actions necessarily lag behind sensory inputs due to delays caused by sensory transduction, axonal conduction, synaptic transmission, and muscle activation.
source: Sensory inputs guide actions, but such actions necessarily lag behind these inputs due to delays caused by sensory transduction, axonal conduction, synaptic transmission, and muscle activation.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about neural processing delays.

claim: A system that parsimoniously predicts future inputs from their past and generalizes well to new inputs is likely to contain representations that reflect their underlying causes.
source: Prediction has other fundamental theoretical advantages: a system that parsimoniously predicts future inputs from their past, and that generalizes well to new inputs, is likely to contain representations that reflect their underlying causes (Bialek et al., 2001).
evidence: This theoretical claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Much of sensory processing involves discarding irrelevant information to arrive at a representation of what is important in the environment for guiding action.
source: Furthermore, much of sensory processing involves discarding irrelevant information, such as that which is not predictive of the future, to arrive at a representation of what is important in the environment for guiding action (Bialek et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous theoretical work.

claim: Previous theoretical studies have suggested that many neural representations can be understood in terms of efficient coding of natural stimuli in a short time window at or just before the present.
source: Previous theoretical studies have suggested that many neural representations can be understood in terms of efficient coding of natural stimuli in a short time window at or just before the present (Attneave, 1954; Barlow, 1959; Olshausen and Field, 1996, Olshausen and Field, 1997).
evidence: This claim summarizes previous work and is supported by multiple citations.

claim: One pioneering study trained a network to efficiently represent static natural images using a sparse, generative model.
source: One pioneering such study trained a network to efficiently represent static natural images using a sparse, generative model (Olshausen and Field, 1996, Olshausen and Field, 1997).
evidence: This describes previous work and is supported by citations.

claim: The timescale of prediction considered for the temporal prediction model is in the range of tens to hundreds of milliseconds.
source: The timescale of prediction considered for our model is in the range of tens to hundreds of milliseconds.
evidence: This is a specification of the model design.

claim: Conduction delays to cortex and very fast motor responses are on the timescale of tens to hundreds of milliseconds.
source: Conduction delays to cortex and very fast motor responses are on this timescale (Bixler et al., 1967; Yeomans and Frankland, 1995; Bizley et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The idea that prediction is an important component of perception dates at least as far back as Helmholtz.
source: The idea that prediction is an important component of perception dates at least as far back as Helmholtz (Helmholtz, 1962; Sutton and Barton, 1981), although what is meant by prediction and the purpose it serves is quite varied between models incorporating it (Chalk et al., 2018; Salisbury and Palmer, 2016).
evidence: This historical claim is supported by citations.

claim: In the predictive coding framework, prediction is used to remove statistical redundancy in order to provide an efficient representation of the entire stimulus.
source: In the 'predictive coding' framework (Huang and Rao, 2011; Rao and Ballard, 1999; Friston, 2003), prediction is used to remove statistical redundancy in order to provide an efficient representation of the entire stimulus.
evidence: This describes a theoretical framework and is supported by citations.

claim: The predictive information framework involves selective encoding of those features of the stimulus that predict future input.
source: In contrast, the 'predictive information' framework (Bialek et al., 2001; Salisbury and Palmer, 2016; Palmer et al., 2015; Heeger, 2017), which our approach relates to more closely, involves selective encoding of those features of the stimulus that predict future input.
evidence: This describes a theoretical framework and is supported by citations.

claim: The predictive coding approach seeks to find a compressed representation of the entire input, whereas the predictive information approach selectively encodes only predictive features.
source: Hence, the predictive coding approach seeks to find a compressed representation of the entire input, whereas the predictive information approach selectivity encodes only predictive features (Chalk et al., 2018; Salisbury and Palmer, 2016).
evidence: This comparison of frameworks is supported by citations.

claim: In mammalian primary visual cortex (V1), neurons typically respond strongly to oriented edge-like structures moving over a particular retinal location.
source: In mammalian primary visual cortex (V1), neurons typically respond strongly to oriented edge-like structures moving over a particular retinal location (Hubel and Wiesel, 1959; Jones and Palmer, 1987; DeAngelis et al., 1993; Ringach, 2002).
evidence: This is established knowledge about V1 neurons supported by citations.

claim: In mammalian primary auditory cortex (A1), most neurons respond strongly to changes in the amplitude of sounds within a certain frequency range.
source: In mammalian primary auditory cortex (A1), most neurons respond strongly to changes in the amplitude of sounds within a certain frequency range (deCharms et al., 1998).
evidence: This is established knowledge about A1 neurons supported by a citation.

claim: Previous models based on sparsity or slowness related principles were successful in accounting for many spatial aspects of V1 RF structure.
source: Previous models, based on sparsity or slowness related principles, were successful in accounting for many spatial aspects of V1 RF structure (Olshausen and Field, 1996, Olshausen and Field, 1997; van Hateren and Ruderman, 1998a; Berkes and Wiskott, 2005; Berkes et al., 2009; van Hateren and van der Schaaf, 1998b), and had some success in accounting for spectral aspects of A1 RF structure (Klein et al., 2003; Carlson et al., 2012; Zhao and Zhaoping, 2011; Cusack and Carlyon, 2004).
evidence: This summarizes previous modeling work and is supported by citations.

claim: Previous models do not account well for the temporal structure of V1 or A1 RFs.
source: However, these models do not account well for the temporal structure of V1 or A1 RFs.
evidence: This is a critical assessment of previous models based on comparison to known neural properties.

claim: For both vision and audition, the envelopes of real neuronal RFs tend to be asymmetric in time, with greater sensitivity to very recent inputs compared to inputs further in the past.
source: Notably, for both vision (Ringach, 2002) and audition (deCharms et al., 1998), the envelopes of real neuronal RFs tend to be asymmetric in time, with greater sensitivity to very recent inputs compared to inputs further in the past.
evidence: This describes a property of real neurons supported by citations.

claim: The RFs predicted by previous models typically show symmetrical temporal envelopes.
source: In contrast, the RFs predicted by previous models (van Hateren and Ruderman, 1998a; Klein et al., 2003; Carlson et al., 2012; Kozlov and Gentner, 2016; Cusack and Carlyon, 2004) typically show symmetrical temporal envelopes, with either approximately flat envelopes over time or a balanced falloff of the envelope over time either side of a peak.
evidence: This is a critical assessment of previous models supported by citations.

claim: The temporal prediction model was built as a feedforward network with a single layer of nonlinear hidden units.
source: To determine what type of sensory RF structures would facilitate predictions of the imminent future, we built a feedforward network model with a single layer of nonlinear hidden units, mapping the inputs to the outputs through weighted connections (Figure 1).
evidence: This describes the model architecture and references Figure 1.

claim: Each hidden unit's output results from a linear mapping from the past input, followed by a monotonic nonlinearity.
source: Each hidden unit's output results from a linear mapping (by input weights) from the past input, followed by a monotonic nonlinearity, much like the classic linear-nonlinear model of sensory neurons (Klein et al., 2003; Carlson et al., 2012; Zhao and Zhaoping, 2011).
evidence: This describes the model architecture and relates it to established models via citations.

claim: The model generates a prediction of the future from a linear mapping from the hidden units' outputs.
source: The model then generates a prediction of the future from a linear mapping (by output weights) from the hidden units' outputs.
evidence: This describes the model architecture.

claim: Decoding from neural response is often well approximated by a linear transformation.
source: This is consistent with the observation that decoding from the neural response is often well approximated by a linear transformation (Eliasmith and Anderson, 2003).
evidence: This justifies a design choice with a citation to previous work.

claim: For vision, the inputs were patches of videos of animals moving in natural settings, and the network was trained to predict the pixel values for one movie frame (40 ms) into the future, based on the seven most recent frames (280 ms).
source: For vision, the inputs were patches of videos of animals moving in natural settings, and we trained the network to predict the pixel values for one movie frame (40 ms) into the future, based on the seven most recent frames (280 ms).
evidence: This describes the training methodology for the visual model.

claim: For audition, the network was trained to predict the next three time steps (15 ms) of cochleagrams of natural sounds based on the 40 most recent time steps (200 ms).
source: For audition, we trained the network to predict the next three time steps (15 ms) of cochleagrams of natural sounds based on the 40 most recent time steps (200 ms).
evidence: This describes the training methodology for the auditory model.

claim: Cochleagrams resemble spectrograms but are adjusted to approximate the auditory nerve representation of sounds.
source: Cochleagrams resemble spectrograms but are adjusted to approximate the auditory nerve representation of sounds (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This defines a technical term used in the study.

claim: During training, sparse L1 weight regularization was used to constrain the network to predict future stimuli in a parsimonious fashion.
source: During training we used sparse, L1 weight regularization (see Equation 3 in Materials and methods) to constrain the network to predict future stimuli in a parsimonious fashion, forcing the network to use as few weights as possible while maintaining an accurate prediction.
evidence: This describes a key aspect of the training methodology.

claim: The sparsity constraint can be viewed as an assumption about the sparse nature of causal dependencies underlying the sensory input.
source: This constraint can be viewed as an assumption about the sparse nature of causal dependencies underlying the sensory input, or alternatively as analogous to the energy and space restrictions of neural connectivity.
evidence: This provides theoretical justification for a design choice.

claim: The sparsity constraint in the temporal prediction model differs from that used in sparse coding models in that it is applied to the weights rather than the activity of the units.
source: Note that this sparsity constraint differs from that used in sparse coding models, in that it is applied to the weights rather than the activity of the units, being more like a constraint on the wiring between neurons than a constraint on their firing rates.
evidence: This distinguishes the current model from previous models.

claim: 114 auditory neurons (including 76 single units) were recorded in A1 and the anterior auditory field (AAF) of 5 anesthetized ferrets.
source: To compare with the model, we recorded responses of 114 auditory neurons (including 76 single units) in A1 and the anterior auditory field (AAF) of 5 anesthetized ferrets (Willmore et al., 2016) and measured their spectrotemporal RFs (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This describes the experimental data collection.

claim: Ferrets are commonly used for auditory research because they are readily trained in a range of sound detection, discrimination or localization tasks.
source: Ferrets are commonly used for auditory research, because they are readily trained in a range of sound detection, discrimination or localization tasks (Nodal and King, 2014), the frequency range of their hearing (approximately 40 Hz–40 kHz [Kavanagh and Kelly, 1988]) overlaps well with (and extends beyond) the human range, and most of their auditory cortex is not buried in a sulcus and hence easily accessible for electrophysiological or optical measurements.
evidence: This justifies the choice of animal model with citations.

claim: The A1 RFs recorded are diverse, with frequency tuning that can be narrowband or broadband, and sometimes showing flanking inhibition.
source: The A1 RFs we recorded are diverse (Figure 2a); their frequency tuning can be narrowband or broadband, and sometimes showing flanking inhibition.
evidence: This describes the experimental observations and references Figure 2a.

claim: In their temporal tuning, A1 RFs tend to weight recent inputs more heavily, with a temporally asymmetric power profile, involving excitation near the present followed by lagging inhibition of a longer duration.
source: In their temporal tuning, A1 RFs tend to weight recent inputs more heavily, with a temporally asymmetric power profile, involving excitation near the present followed by lagging inhibition of a longer duration (deCharms et al., 1998).
evidence: This describes a property of real A1 neurons supported by a citation.

claim: The temporal prediction model RFs are similarly diverse to A1 RFs, showing all of the RF types seen in vivo.
source: The temporal prediction model RFs (Figure 2b) are similarly diverse, showing all of the RF types seen in vivo (including examples of localized, narrowband, broadband, complex, disordered and directional RFs) and are well matched in scale and form to those measured in A1.
evidence: This is a key finding comparing model to data, referencing Figure 2b.

claim: The temporal prediction model RFs have greater power near the present, with brief excitation followed by longer lagging inhibition, producing an asymmetric power profile.
source: This includes having greater power (mean square) near the present, with brief excitation followed by longer lagging inhibition, producing an asymmetric power profile.
evidence: This describes a key property of the model RFs that matches real neurons.

claim: Previous attempts to model RFs based on efficient coding, sparse coding and slow feature hypotheses either did not capture the diversity of RFs or lacked temporal asymmetry, punctate structure, or appropriate time scale.
source: This stands in contrast to previous attempts to model RFs based on efficient coding,sparsecoding and slow feature hypotheses, which either did not capture the diversity of RFs (Zhao and Zhaoping, 2011), or lacked temporal asymmetry, punctate structure, or appropriate time scale (Klein et al., 2003; Carlson et al., 2012; Kozlov and Gentner, 2016; Cusack and Carlyon, 2004; Carlin and Elhilali, 2013; Brito and Gerstner, 2016).
evidence: This is a critical comparison to previous models supported by citations.

claim: Substantial similarities were apparent when comparing the temporal prediction model's RFs trained using visual inputs with the 3D and 2D spatiotemporal RFs of real V1 simple cells.
source: By eye, substantial similarities were also apparent when we compared the temporal prediction model's RFs trained using visual inputs (Figure 1b) with the 3D (space-space-time) and 2D (space-time) spatiotemporal RFs of real V1 simple cells, which were obtained from Ohzawa et al (Ohzawa et al., 1996).
evidence: This describes a qualitative comparison between model and data, referencing figures and citing the data source.

claim: Simple cells have stereotyped RFs containing parallel, spatially localized excitatory and inhibitory regions, with each cell having a particular preferred orientation and spatial frequency.
source: Simple cells (Hubel and Wiesel, 1959) have stereotyped RFs containing parallel, spatially localized excitatory and inhibitory regions, with each cell having a particular preferred orientation and spatial frequency (Jones and Palmer, 1987; DeAngelis et al., 1993; Ringach, 2002) (Figure 2c).
evidence: This describes properties of simple cells supported by citations and references Figure 2c.

claim: The features of simple cells are clearly apparent in the model RFs.
source: These features are also clearly apparent in the model RFs (Figure 2d).
evidence: This is a finding based on comparison of model to data, referencing Figure 2d.

claim: Unlike previous models, the temporal prediction model captures the temporal asymmetry of real RFs.
source: Unlike previous models (van Hateren and Ruderman, 1998a; Hyvärinen et al., 2003; Olshausen, 2003), the temporal prediction model captures the temporal asymmetry of real RFs.
evidence: This is a key finding distinguishing the current model from previous work, supported by citations.

claim: The RF power is highest near the present and decays into the past in the temporal prediction model.
source: The RF power is highest near the present and decays into the past (Figure 2d), as observed in real neurons (Ohzawa et al., 1996) (Figure 2c).
evidence: This describes a property of the model RFs that matches real neurons, referencing figures and citing data.

claim: Simple cell RFs have two types of spatiotemporal structure: space-time separable RFs and space-time inseparable RFs.
source: Furthermore, simple cell RFs have two types of spatiotemporal structure: space-time separable RFs (Figure 2cI), whose optimal stimulus resembles a flashing or slowly ramping grating, and space-time inseparable RFs, whose optimal stimulus is a drifting grating (DeAngelis et al., 1993) (Figure 2cII).
evidence: This describes properties of simple cells supported by a citation and references figures.

claim: The temporal prediction model captures the diversity of space-time separable and inseparable RFs.
source: Our model captures this diversity (Figure 2dI–III separable, Figure 2dIV–VI inseparable).
evidence: This is a finding based on analysis of model RFs, referencing figures.

claim: A sparse coding model was trained using the same dataset as the temporal prediction model for comparison.
source: For comparison, we trained a sparse coding model (Olshausen and Field, 1996, Olshausen and Field, 1997; Carlson et al., 2012) (https://github.com/zayd/sparsenet) using our dataset.
evidence: This describes a control experiment using an established model.

claim: The sparse coding model would be expected to perform less well in the temporal domain because the direction of time is not explicitly accounted for.
source: We would expect such a model to perform less well in the temporal domain, because unlike the temporal prediction model, the direction of time is not explicitly accounted for.
evidence: This is a prediction based on theoretical understanding of the models.

claim: The sparse coding model has set the standard for normative models of visual RFs and has also been applied for auditory RFs.
source: The sparse coding model was chosen because it has set the standard for normative models of visual RFs (Olshausen and Field, 1996, Olshausen, 2003; Olshausen and Field, 1997), and the same model has also been applied for auditory RFs (Carlson et al., 2012; Brito and Gerstner, 2016; Młynarski and McDermott, 2017; Blättler et al., 2011).
evidence: This justifies the choice of control model with citations.

claim: The RFs of the sparse coding model span a much larger region than the real A1 and temporal prediction model RFs in the multi-dimensional scaling space.
source: The RFs of the sparse coding model span a much larger region than the real A1 and temporal prediction model RFs.
evidence: This is a finding from the MDS analysis shown in Figure 6a.

claim: The A1 and temporal prediction model RFs occupy a similar region of the MDS space, indicating their greater similarity to each other relative to those of the sparse coding model.
source: Furthermore, the A1 and temporal prediction model RFs occupy a similar region of the space, indicating their greater similarity to each other relative to those of the sparse coding model.
evidence: This is a finding from the MDS analysis shown in Figure 6a.

claim: For the data and the temporal prediction model, most of the power is contained in the most recent time-steps.
source: We first considered the temporal properties of the RFs and found that for the data and the temporal prediction model, most of the power is contained in the most recent time-steps (Figures 2a–b, 3–4 and 6b, and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding referencing multiple figures.

claim: The sparse coding model does not show the feature of having most power in the most recent time-steps.
source: Given that the direction of time is not explicitly accounted for in the sparse coding model, as expected, it does not show this feature (Figures 5 and 6b).
evidence: This is a finding about the control model referencing figures.

claim: In the real data, neurons tend to show leading excitation followed by lagging inhibition of longer duration.
source: In the time domain, the real data tend to show leading excitation followed by lagging inhibition of longer duration (Figures 2a, 3 and 6c–e).
evidence: This describes a property of real neurons referencing figures.

claim: The temporal prediction model shows many RFs with leading excitation followed by lagging inhibition of longer duration than the leading excitation.
source: The temporal prediction model also shows many RFs with this temporal structure, with lagging inhibition of longer duration than the leading excitation (Figures 2b, 4 and 6c–e, and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding about the model RFs referencing figures.

claim: The sparse coding model does not show the stereotyped temporal structure of leading excitation followed by longer lagging inhibition.
source: This is not the case with the sparse coding model, where units tend to show either excitation and inhibition having the same duration or an elongated temporal structure that does not show such stereotyped polarity changes (Figures 5 and 6c–e).
evidence: This is a finding about the control model referencing figures.

claim: The absolute timescales of excitation and inhibition match the data more closely in the case of the temporal prediction model.
source: It is also the case that the absolute timescales of excitation and inhibition match the data more closely in the case of the temporal prediction model (Figure 6c–e), although a few units display inhibition of a longer duration than is seen in the data (Figure 6c).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding referencing figures.

claim: The sparse coding model shows a wide range of temporal spans of excitation and inhibition, in keeping with previous studies.
source: The sparse coding model shows a wide range of temporal spans of excitation and inhibition, in keeping with previous studies (Carlson et al., 2012; Carlin and Elhilali, 2013).
evidence: This describes a property of the control model and relates it to previous work via citations.

claim: In real neuronal RFs, the spans of inhibition and excitation over sound frequency tend to be similar.
source: Regarding the spectral properties of real neuronal RFs, the spans of inhibition and excitation over sound frequency tend to be similar (Figure 6f–h).
evidence: This describes a property of real neurons referencing figures.

claim: The temporal prediction model shows similar spans of inhibition and excitation over sound frequency, albeit with slightly more variation.
source: This is also seen in the temporal prediction model, albeit with slightly more variation (Figure 6f–h).
evidence: This is a finding about the model referencing figures.

claim: The sparse coding model shows more extensive variation in frequency spans than either the data or the temporal prediction model.
source: The sparse coding model shows more extensive variation in frequency spans than either the data or our model (Figure 6f–h).
evidence: This is a finding about the control model referencing figures.

claim: In both the neural data and the temporal prediction model, most power is in the most recent time steps.
source: We compared temporal properties of the RFs from the neural data and the temporal prediction model. In both cases, most power (mean over space and neurons of squared values) is in the most recent time steps (Figure 7a).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding referencing Figure 7a.

claim: Previous normative models of spatiotemporal RFs do not show the property of having most power in the most recent time steps.
source: Previous normative models of spatiotemporal RFs (van Hateren and Ruderman, 1998a; Hyvärinen et al., 2003; Olshausen, 2003) (Figure 7—figure supplement 1c–d) do not show this property, being either invariant over time or localized, but with a symmetric profile that is not restricted to the recent past.
evidence: This is a comparison to previous models supported by citations and referencing figures.

claim: The temporal prediction model produced substantial numbers of both space-time separable and inseparable units (631 separable, 969 inseparable).
source: We also measured the space-time separability of the RFs of the temporal prediction model (see Materials and methods); substantial numbers of both space-time separable and inseparable units were apparent (631 separable, 969 inseparable; Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding about the model referencing a figure.

claim: The mean tilt direction index (TDI) for the temporal prediction model population was 0.34 (0.29 SD), comparable with the ranges in the neural data.
source: The mean TDI for the population was 0.34 (0.29 SD), comparable with the ranges in the neural data (mean 0.16; 0.12 SD in cat area 17/18 (Baker, 2001), mean 0.51; 0.30 SD in macaque V1 [Livingstone and Conway, 2007]).
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison between model and data supported by citations.

claim: An inverse correlation (r2 = −0.33, p<10−9, n = 1205) was observed between temporal and spatial frequency tuning in the temporal prediction model.
source: Finally, we observed an inverse correlation (r2 = −0.33, p<10−9, n = 1205) between temporal and spatial frequency tuning (See Materials and methods), which is also a property of real V1 RFs (DeAngelis et al., 1993) and is seen in a sparse-coding-related model (van Hateren and Ruderman, 1998a).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding about the model that matches real neurons, supported by citations.

claim: The spatial tuning characteristics of the temporal prediction model's RFs displayed a wide range of orientation and spatial frequency preferences, consistent with the neural data.
source: The spatial tuning characteristics of the temporal prediction model's RFs displayed a wide range of orientation and spatial frequency preferences, consistent with the neural data (DeAngelis et al., 1993; Kreile et al., 2011) (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a finding about the model compared to data, supported by citations and referencing a figure.

claim: Both model and real RFs show a preference for spatial orientations along the horizontal and vertical axes.
source: Both model and real RFs (Kreile et al., 2011) show a preference for spatial orientations along the horizontal and vertical axes, although this orientation bias is seen to a greater extent in the temporal prediction model than in the data.
evidence: This is a finding comparing model to data, supported by a citation.

claim: The widths and lengths of the RFs of the temporal prediction model, relative to the period of their oscillation, match the neural data well.
source: Furthermore, the widths and lengths of the RFs of the temporal prediction model, relative to the period of their oscillation, also match the neural data well (Figure 7d).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding referencing Figure 7d.

claim: Only the temporal prediction model seems to be able to capture the blob-like RFs that form a sizeable proportion of the neural data.
source: Although this property is again fairly well captured by previous models (Olshausen and Field, 1996, Olshausen and Field, 1997; Berkes et al., 2009; Ringach, 2002; van Hateren and van der Schaaf, 1998b) (Figure 7—figure supplement 1g), only the temporal prediction model seems to be able to capture the blob-like RFs that form a sizeable proportion of the neural data (Ringach, 2002) (Figure 7d where nx and ny < ~0.25, Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a finding distinguishing the current model from previous models, supported by citations and referencing figures.

claim: Under the hypothesis of temporal prediction, the better the temporal prediction model network is at predicting the future, the more the RFs of the network should resemble those of real neurons.
source: Under our hypothesis of temporal prediction, we would expect that the better the temporal prediction model network is at predicting the future, the more the RFs of the network should resemble those of real neurons.
evidence: This is a prediction derived from the hypothesis.

claim: The set of hyperparameter settings that give good predictions are also those where the temporal prediction model produces RFs that are most similar to those recorded in A1 (r2 = 0.8, p<10−9, n = 55).
source: The set of hyperparameter settings that give good predictions are also those where the temporal prediction model produces RFs that are most similar to those recorded in A1 (r2 = 0.8, p<10−9, n = 55).
evidence: This is a key quantitative finding supporting the hypothesis.

claim: The result that better prediction correlates with greater similarity to neural RFs argues that cortical neurons are indeed optimized for temporal prediction.
source: This result argues that cortical neurons are indeed optimized for temporal prediction.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the correlation between prediction accuracy and similarity to neural data.

claim: When the similarity measure was examined as a function of hyperparameters for the sparse coding model, a monotonic relationship between stimulus reconstruction capacity and similarity of real RFs was not found (r2 = −0.05, p=0.69, n = 50).
source: When the similarity measure was examined as a function of the same hyperparameters for the sparse coding model (Figure 8—figure supplement 1), and this was compared to that model's stimulus reconstruction capacity as a function of the same hyperparameters, a monotonic relationship between stimulus reconstruction capacity and similarity of real RFs was not found (Figure 8—figure supplement 1; r2 = −0.05, p=0.69, n = 50).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding about the control model referencing a figure.

claim: The temporal prediction model provides an independent criterion, the prediction error, to perform hyperparameter selection.
source: In contrast, the temporal prediction model provides an independent criterion, the prediction error, to perform hyperparameter selection.
evidence: This highlights an advantage of the temporal prediction model.

claim: No such effective, measurable, independent criterion for hyperparameter selection has been proposed for other normative models of RFs.
source: To our knowledge, no such effective, measurable, independent criterion for hyperparameter selection has been proposed for other normative models of RFs.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the approach based on knowledge of the field.

claim: When the regularization is at the optimum for prediction, the auditory and visual model RFs qualitatively most closely resemble those of A1 neurons and V1 simple cells, respectively.
source: When the regularization strength is at the optimum for prediction, the auditory and visual model RFs qualitatively most closely resemble those of A1 neurons and V1 simple cells, respectively.
evidence: This is a finding about the relationship between model performance and similarity to neural data.

claim: Examining the relationship between predictive capacity and sparsity over the range of L1 weight regularization strength and hidden units explored, a clear monotonic relationship was not found.
source: Examining the relationship between predictive capacity and sparsity, over the range of L1 weight regularization strength and hidden units explored, we did not find a clear monotonic relationship.
evidence: This is a finding about the relationship between prediction and sparsity in the model.

claim: In both the auditory and visual cases, the hidden unit and L1 regularization combination with the best prediction had intermediate sparsity.
source: Indeed, in both the auditory and visual cases, the hidden unit and L1 regularization combination with the best prediction had intermediate sparsity.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding about the model.

claim: For both the auditory and visual models, when a different hidden unit nonlinearity (tanh or rectified linear) was used, the networks had similar predictive capacity and produced comparable RFs.
source: For both the auditory and visual models, when a different hidden unit nonlinearity (tanh or rectified linear) was used, the networks had similar predictive capacity and produced comparable RFs.
evidence: This describes a robustness test of the model.

claim: When the temporal prediction model had linear hidden units, it no longer predicted as well and produced RFs that were less like real neurons in their structure.
source: However, when the temporal prediction model had linear hidden units, it no longer predicted as well and produced RFs that were less like real neurons in their structure.
evidence: This describes a control experiment showing the importance of nonlinearity.

claim: The temporal prediction model and sparse coding model results were trained on inputs with added Gaussian noise (6 dB SNR), mimicking inherent noise in the nervous system.
source: The temporal prediction model and sparse coding model results shown in the main figures of this paper were trained on inputs with added Gaussian noise (6 dB SNR), mimicking inherent noise in the nervous system.
evidence: This describes a methodological choice in the study.

claim: All models were also trained without noise, producing similar results.
source: To determine the effect of adding this noise, all models were also trained without noise, producing similar results (Figure 4—figure supplements 5–7; Figure 5—figure supplements 3–5; Figure 6—figure supplement 1; Figure 7—figure supplements 2–3).
evidence: This describes a control experiment referencing figures.

claim: The results were robust to changes in the duration of the temporal window being predicted.
